title: unstakeFor function is entirely absent from the migration plan and routes NFTs to the migrator, not the beneficiary
description: The migration plan's 'NFTStakerV2 deltas' section enumerates exactly two surgical additions: `stakeFor(beneficiary, amount)` and `withdrawRewardToken(to, amount)`. `unstakeFor` is not mentioned anywhere in the plan. The migration is documented as one-way (id-4 -> id-6) with end users calling `oldStaker.unstake(amount)` themselves on the V1 staker side; there is no design rationale for the V2 staker needing a migrator-driven unstake path. The implementation adds `unstakeFor` (line 543) which transfers the NFTs to `msg.sender` (the migrator) at line 558, not to the beneficiary. The pending phUSD does correctly route to the beneficiary via the refactored `_safePay(beneficiary, pending)`, but the principal NFTs land in the migrator's wallet. Combined with the unplanned `onlyOwnerOrMigrator` access on `withdrawRewardToken` (see ECON-01), the migrator can: (a) pull any beneficiary's NFTs to themselves via `unstakeFor`, (b) drive `totalStaked` to zero, (c) trigger pause and drain the phUSD reward budget.
impact: The migrator role acquires powers strictly beyond what the plan describes. A user who stakes via `stakeFor` does not consent to the migrator subsequently being able to withdraw their NFTs. There is no on-chain documentation (NatSpec, README, comment) explaining why `unstakeFor` exists or what its intended trust model is. Magnitude: the migrator can extract every NFT held by every beneficiary in a single sequence of calls, capped only by gas and the migrator's willingness to pause-and-drain. For the documented migration of ~139 id-4 NFTs, the migrator can claim the full set of post-migration id-6 NFTs.
recommendation: Either (a) remove `unstakeFor` and `UnstakedFor` event entirely — it is not required by the migration plan and beneficiaries can use the standard `unstake` path themselves; or (b) keep `unstakeFor` but route the NFT transfer to the beneficiary (`stakedToken.safeTransferFrom(address(this), beneficiary, ...)`) instead of `msg.sender`, eliminating the principal-redirection vector; or (c) keep current behaviour but add an explicit beneficiary consent gate (e.g., a per-user opt-in flag or a signature). The plan-as-written supports option (a).
attack_scenario:
1. Owner deploys NFTStakerV2, sets migrator = MigrationHelper, funds runway, sets targetAPY = 0.3e18.
2. Users migrate via `migrationHelper.migrateAndStake(amount)`; helper holds id-6 NFTs briefly and calls `staker.stakeFor(user, amount)` — beneficiary records show staked NFTs.
3. Later, owner rotates migrator (e.g., for a future incident) via `setMigrator(newMigrator)`. If newMigrator is a contract with a function `pullEverything()` (or is an EOA), it can iterate over known stakers (read from on-chain `users[beneficiary]` mapping after enumerating Staked/StakedFor events) and call `unstakeFor(beneficiary, users[beneficiary].amount)` for each. Each call sends NFTs to newMigrator.
4. Once totalStaked == 0, newMigrator (with cooperation from pauser, or self if migrator == pauser by misconfiguration) calls `pause()` and then `withdrawRewardToken(newMigrator, fullBalance)`.
5. Net outcome: newMigrator holds every staked id-6 NFT plus the full phUSD balance; beneficiaries have stale `users[beneficiary]` entries with zero amount and only the in-flight pending paid out during the unstakeFor call.

Note: ALL steps require the owner to have set the migrator role to the eventual extractor. This is the unintended-privilege framing: the plan never authorised the migrator to hold this combination of powers, so an honest owner could grant the role in good faith to a helper later found to be misbehaving.
